title: Hundreds of Everyday AI Apps Secretly Embed Sexual Deepfake Abuse, Warns WIRED Investigation
body:
A recent investigation has revealed that dozens of seemingly innocuous artificial‑intelligence applications are concealing hidden functions that enable the creation of violent and sexually abusive deep‑fake imagery. Researchers identified roughly 400 apps and websites—most of them originating from Chinese‑language developers—that market themselves as everyday tools for tasks such as pet portrait generation, photo enhancement, or text‑to‑image art. Behind their benign façades, many of these platforms contain undocumented “secret modes” that allow users to produce graphic, non‑consensual content, raising urgent questions about the effectiveness of current app‑store vetting processes and the broader challenge of policing AI‑generated media.

The investigation began with a popular pet‑portrait app called Viefur, which advertises a simple coin‑based system: users purchase digital credits for about US$4, each credit unlocking a set number of AI‑generated pet pictures. While the app’s primary function appears to be harmless—turning a dog or cat photo into a stylized illustration—researchers discovered a concealed menu that, when activated, switched the underlying model from a benign style transfer to a “NSFW” mode. In this hidden setting, the same algorithm could be repurposed to generate explicit or violent images of people, effectively turning a pet‑filter into a deep‑fake weapon.

Further digging uncovered a pattern across a wide range of applications. Many of the apps, which include language‑learning assistants, background‑removal tools, and even simple meme generators, embed a secondary API endpoint that is not listed in public documentation. By sending a specific request string—often a single hidden keyword—users can unlock a “dark” version of the model capable of producing pornographic or gore‑laden content. Some platforms even offered a “premium” tier that promised higher‑resolution outputs for a higher price, effectively monetising the creation of illicit material.

The scale of the problem is amplified by the way these apps reach consumers. Most are distributed through major mobile marketplaces such as Google Play and Apple’s App Store, as well as Chinese Android stores that have looser content‑moderation policies. Because the illicit features are not advertised, they evade the automated scans that app‑store operators typically run on descriptions, screenshots, and sample media. Only a handful of users who accidentally discovered the hidden menus reported the issue, allowing the developers to keep the dark functionality under the radar.

Cyber‑security experts warn that the presence of such covert capabilities could have far‑reaching consequences. Deep‑fake technology already poses a threat to personal privacy, political stability, and the integrity of visual evidence. When the creation of non‑consensual sexual or violent imagery is embedded in everyday tools, the barrier to producing harmful content drops dramatically. Victims could find themselves targeted by synthetic pornography or violent hoaxes without ever having interacted with the original app, complicating law‑enforcement investigations and legal recourse.

Regulators and platform owners are now facing pressure to tighten oversight. In the United States, the bipartisan “DEEPFAKE Accountability Act” is moving through Congress, proposing stricter disclosure requirements for AI‑generated media and heavier penalties for developers who embed malicious functions. Meanwhile, Apple and Google have announced internal reviews of their AI‑related app categories, pledging faster takedowns for apps that violate content policies. However, the technical nature of hidden APIs makes detection difficult; it may require more proactive auditing, including reverse‑engineering of app binaries and mandatory reporting of all model capabilities to a central registry.

As AI tools become ever more accessible, the line between creative assistance and weaponisation blurs. The uncovered network of covert deep‑fake features underscores the need for a coordinated response that blends technology, policy, and user education. Industry stakeholders must adopt transparent development practices, while governments should consider clearer standards for AI content moderation. Only through collective vigilance can the promise of generative AI be preserved without sacrificing the safety and dignity of individuals worldwide.
